intro.title: The standards and regulations you work to
intro.body: Here you see each standard and regulation your organisation follows, and how much of it is documented. The number in the ring is the **[[requirement-coverage|requirement coverage]]**: the share of requirements shown by evidence from the work you already do.
steps: Turn on the standards that apply to you. Start with the ones customers or authorities ask about.
Open a standard and go through its requirements. Link risks, documents, suppliers and other records as **evidence**.
Use “Gaps” to see what is left, and “Recommended next step” inside the standard to know what to do now.

why.body: Auditors and authorities check every requirement that applies to you. When evidence is linked while you work, you are audit-ready all year, and one record often covers several standards at once.

intro.title: What requirement coverage tells you
intro.body: [[requirement-coverage|Requirement coverage]] sums up how well prepared you are for an audit or an inspection. It only counts requirements that apply to you, and recent evidence counts more than old evidence.
steps: Look first at requirements nobody has started. Click the number to open them.
Then renew evidence that is older than a year or still only a draft.
Export the requirement matrix when the auditor asks for it, or build an audit pack under Reports.

why.body: The ISO standards require you to monitor and evaluate the management system and review it at management level. Coverage per standard is a simple, verifiable input to that review.

intro.title: How to work with a standard
intro.body: The standard is split into **clauses**, and each clause has one or more **requirements**. For each requirement you show with **evidence** that you meet it: a procedure, a risk assessment, a training record or another record you already have in CoreFlow.
steps: Follow “Recommended next step” at the top, or open a requirement from the contents.
Link records you have, or create a new one right from the requirement. One record can cover every requirement of a clause.

Give the requirement an owner and a target date, and mark it reviewed once you have checked it. A requirement can only be marked not applicable where the standard allows it, and always with a justification.

why.body: What the auditor wants to see is the chain: the requirement, who owns it, and the evidence that shows it is followed. When everything is linked here, you can answer every question in one click.

intro.title: What is missing
intro.body: These are the requirements that apply to you but have no confirmed evidence yet. Each one shows which records would close the gap.
steps: Pick a chapter to work on one part of the standard at a time.
Create the record that closes the gap. It is linked to the requirement automatically.
Open the requirement if you already have a record that documents it.

sections.heading: A requirement is something you must do
sections.body: A standard is a list of **requirements**: things the organisation must do or have in place. CoreFlow shows them clause by clause, with a plain-language explanation alongside.

sections.heading: Evidence shows that you do it
sections.body: **Evidence** is records you already have: a procedure, a risk assessment, a supplier evaluation, a training record. Once a record is linked and confirmed, the requirement is **covered**. Drafts and documents past their review date only count as partly covered.

sections.heading: Not every requirement applies to everyone
sections.body: Some requirements can be marked **not applicable** with a short justification, for example an Annex A control that does not fit your business. Clauses 4–10 of the ISO standards, however, cannot be excluded. In ISO 9001, requirements in clause 8 can only be excluded when the scope (4.3) justifies it.

sections.heading: Owners and target dates
sections.body: Give each requirement an **owner** and a **target date**. Then everyone knows who follows it up, and the auditor sees that someone owns it. Mark the requirement **reviewed** once you have checked that the evidence still holds.

quiz.question: You linked a draft procedure as evidence. What is the requirement's status?
quiz.explanation: A draft is weak evidence: it shows the work has started, not that it is approved and in use. The requirement is partly covered until the procedure is approved.

sections.heading: Only requirements that apply to you count
sections.body: Requirements you marked not applicable, with a justification, are left out. The number shows what you actually have to do.

sections.heading: Evidence makes a requirement covered
sections.body: Many requirements have a place in CoreFlow **where you fill this in**, for example a register or a plan. When that place is complete, the requirement is covered; when it is only partly filled in, the requirement is partly covered. Requirements without such a place are covered when at least one confirmed record documents it. You can also set the status yourself, with a note saying why. A partly covered requirement counts half.

sections.heading: Recent evidence counts in full
sections.body: Evidence confirmed or updated within the last year counts in full. Older evidence counts 60 %, because auditors expect records to be kept up to date.

quiz.question: A requirement is covered by an approved procedure that was last changed two years ago and is not yet due for review. How much does it count?
quiz.explanation: The requirement is still covered, but the evidence is older than a year, so it counts 60 %. Review the procedure to make it count in full again. A document past its review date counts only as partly covered.

overview.title: One standard per card
overview.body: The ring shows the requirement coverage. Below it you see how many requirements are covered, and each chapter on its own.

overview.title: Coverage details
overview.body: See what the number is made of, open the requirements behind each part, and export the requirement matrix.

overview.title: More standards
overview.body: Turn on more standards here. Evidence you have already linked often helps in the new standard too.

clause-kind-annex-control.definition: A safeguard from the list in Annex A of ISO/IEC 27001 or ISO/IEC 42001. You decide in the Statement of Applicability which controls apply.

clause-kind-article.definition: A provision of an EU regulation or directive, for example GDPR Article 30.

clause-kind-recital.definition: The introductory reasoning of an EU act. Recitals set no requirements themselves, but explain how the articles are to be read.

clause-kind-annex.definition: A part at the end of the act or standard with lists and details that the articles or clauses refer to.

evidence.definition: A record in CoreFlow that shows a requirement is met, for example an approved procedure, a risk assessment or a training record.

soa.definition: The overview of which Annex A controls apply to you, why, and how far they are implemented. It is made in the risk module and decides applicability here.

licensed-copy.definition: Standard texts are protected by copyright. CoreFlow shows its own explanations. If you have bought the standard, you can upload your own PDF to see the official text alongside.

shared-iso-clause.definition: Clauses 4–10 are the same in every ISO management-system standard. Evidence for a shared clause therefore helps in every standard you have turned on.
